meta.blurb: Hana walked fast for a living, and now that she has retired she still cannot slow down. Then she meets Samir, who strolls the river path at a snail's pace. Beside him she learns to breathe as if each breath were new.
meta.bible: Hana Kovacs: a retired postwoman of sixty-four, used to walking fast along her Round every day. Samir: her quiet neighbour, a retired carpenter who walks very slowly along the river path each morning. Mei: Hana's granddaughter, about seven, curious and playful. Hana's sister Edith: they quarrelled and have not spoken for a year. Mrs Okoro: a neighbour who joins the walks with her small dog, Biscuit. Teo: a teenage boy who joins with his headphones around his neck. The story takes place in one small town beside a River, with a Path along the water, a Bench, a Bridge and a hill with a view, over about one year from spring to the next spring. Key terms: Breath, Diaphragm, Belly breathing, Walking, Rhythm, Senses, Pilgrimage. Facts are hedged: at rest an adult breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute; slow breathing helps many people feel calmer, but studies differ and it is not a treatment. Traditions: Buddhist monasteries alternate sitting with slow walking; the Camino de Santiago in Spain is a pilgrim route, about eight hundred kilometres on the French Way; pilgrims at Mecca walk around the Kaaba; the labyrinth in Chartres Cathedral in France dates from about the year 1200. The words Spiritus in Latin, Ruach in Hebrew, Pneuma in Greek and Prana in Sanskrit are all linked to breath, wind or spirit. Voice and tone: slow, warm, concrete and a little humorous; one clear idea in each beat; nothing is forced and nothing is promised. Beat 50 reminds the reader that this book is general information and that anyone with breathing difficulties or who feels very low or anxious for a long time should speak to a doctor.

B1B2: Hana has just retired after forty years as a postwoman, and she wakes up with nothing to do. She still walks fast along the river, as if there were letters in her bag.
Hana passes her neighbour Samir, a retired carpenter, who is walking very slowly with his hands behind his back. He nods to her, and she thinks that he must be tired.
Next day Hana joins Samir and tries to match his slow steps. He asks where she is going, and she answers that she is going nowhere, so he asks why she is hurrying.
Samir explains that most of us treat walking as a way to get somewhere else. He suggests that each step can be an arrival in itself.
Before they walk, Samir asks Hana to stand quite still and feel her feet. She notices how her weight rests on the ground and how it shifts from side to side.
Samir shows her a very simple rhythm for the walk. They take one slow step while they breathe in, and one slow step while they breathe out, and they never push the breath.
As she walks, Hana's mind fills with lists of shopping, bills and jobs for the weekend. Each time she notices, she comes back to the feeling of her feet and her breath.
Samir tells Hana that an adult at rest usually breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute. We do this all day and all night, and hardly ever notice it.
Samir points out that breathing is a very unusual part of the body. It works by itself while we sleep, but we can also take charge of it whenever we choose.
Samir explains the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle underneath the lungs. When it moves down, the lungs fill with air, and the belly gently rises.
Hana sits on the bench with one hand on her belly. She breathes in slowly and feels her hand rise, and then she breathes out and feels it fall.
Samir says that a longer out-breath helps many people to feel calmer. Studies suggest that slow breathing can relax the body, although the results are not the same for everyone.
Samir says that it is usually best to breathe in through the nose when walking gently. The nose warms the air, adds moisture to it and catches some of the dust.
Samir teaches Hana a very simple count to use. She breathes in for four steps and out for six, and if it feels uncomfortable she lets the numbers go.
Samir has one rule that he repeats often: never force the breath. If a pattern makes her feel anxious or uncomfortable, Hana is free to stop and simply breathe as she likes.
Walking slowly, Hana feels how each step rolls from the heel through the middle of the foot to the toes. She had never noticed this small movement in all her years of walking.
On the path they stop and listen to what is around them. Hana hears water running over stones, a blackbird singing and the wind in the reeds.
Samir invites Hana to look closely at one leaf. She sees the pattern of its veins, the tiny holes where an insect has eaten, and the way the light passes through.
After a spring shower, the whole river path smells of wet earth and wild garlic. Hana stops, breathes in deeply and smiles like a child.
On the open stretch of the path, Hana holds her hands out to the sun. She feels the warmth on her skin and the cool wind on her face at the same moment.
Samir suggests that Hana choose one sense each day to listen to with special care. On Monday it is hearing, on Tuesday sight, and on Wednesday touch.
Hana often loses her place and starts thinking about something else. She has learned to smile at herself and begin again, without scolding.
One morning it rains, and Hana wants to go home. Samir suggests that they walk anyway, and she finds that the cold drops on her face change from moment to moment.
One morning Hana leaves her watch at home on the kitchen table. By the end of the week she realises that she has hardly missed it, and her days feel much longer.
Hana worries that walking slowly is a kind of laziness. Samir tells her that it is not, and that a person can be fully present at any speed, even when running for a bus.
Samir tells Hana that in many Buddhist monasteries, monks alternate sitting meditation with slow walking meditation. They walk back and forth, paying attention to each step.
Samir also tells her about pilgrimage, which means a long walk for a spiritual reason. Each year people walk the Camino de Santiago in Spain, and pilgrims at Mecca walk around the Kaaba.
Samir describes the labyrinth in Chartres Cathedral in France, which dates from about the year 1200. Visitors can walk its winding path slowly to the centre and back again, as a kind of quiet prayer.
Samir tells Hana something curious about old words from many different places. The Latin spiritus, the Hebrew ruach, the Greek pneuma and the Sanskrit prana are all linked to breath, wind or spirit.
Hana's granddaughter Mei, who is about seven, comes to visit. She turns slow walking into a game, and they see who can walk the most slowly without stopping.
At home, Hana decides to climb the stairs slowly. She feels each foot land, notices her legs working and finds that her breath settles by the top.
Standing at the bus stop, Hana used to sigh and look at her watch. Now she feels her feet, takes three slow breaths and looks at the sky.
Hana has not spoken to her sister Edith for a year after a quarrel. Before she dials the number, she sits down, feels her feet and breathes slowly.
Edith answers, and for a moment neither sister can speak. The call is awkward at first, but it is kind, and they agree to meet at the weekend.
On the anniversary of her husband's death, Hana walks slowly with her sadness instead of trying to push it away. The breath does not remove the grief, but it gives it room.
A cyclist whizzes past so close that Hana nearly falls. Anger flares in her chest, but she takes a long breath and lets her out-breath carry it away.
At home Hana waters her plants slowly, one pot at a time. She watches the water soak into the soil and notices the smell of green leaves.
One cold morning Hana feels very tired and heavy in her legs. Samir says that resting is part of the practice, and he reminds her never to push when her body needs a break.
Hana's neighbour has asthma, and she asks Samir if breathing slowly could replace her medicine. Samir says no, and that anyone with breathing difficulties should see a doctor.
One morning they climb the hill above the town. They go slowly, matching each step to a breath, and they stop whenever the view invites them to.
From the top of the hill, Hana can see the whole river and the rooftops of the town. She feels calm, and the view feels like a gift that she has earned slowly.
At the top of the hill Samir tells Hana that he used to hurry too. He was a young carpenter who always rushed, until his grandfather taught him to walk slowly.
Soon more people from the street join the morning walk. Mrs Okoro comes with her little dog, Biscuit, and Teo, a teenage boy, comes with headphones around his neck.
Some mornings the group walks without speaking at all. Hana is surprised to find that the silence feels like company, and not like emptiness.
One summer evening they walk beside the river after dark. The lights of the town shine on the water, and the first stars appear above the hill.
In winter, the river path is white with frost, and the walkers can see their breath rising in clouds. Hana finds it wonderful to see the air that she has always breathed.
In January Hana catches a bad cold and stays at home for a whole week. When she returns to the path, nobody is cross, and she feels no guilt at all.
Hana begins to bring the practice into her day. She takes three slow breaths at the front door, before answering her phone and before she sits down to eat.
A year has passed, and spring has come to the river path again. Samir says that the path was never for getting anywhere, and Hana walks on with Mei.
Walk slowly, breathe easily, notice what is around you and arrive again at every step. This book is not medical advice, so please see a doctor if you have trouble breathing.
C1C2: Having carried the post through every kind of weather for forty years, Hana woke up on her first morning of retirement with an empty day ahead of her and no idea what to do with it. Out of long habit she strode along the river path at her old, brisk pace, as though a heavy bag of letters still hung from her shoulder. She was going nowhere, but she was going there very fast, and she did not yet see how strange that was.

On the third morning, Hana overtook her neighbour Samir, a retired carpenter, who was walking beside the water at a pace that would have embarrassed a snail. His hands were clasped behind his back and his face was calm, and when he nodded to her she wondered whether he was unwell. She would soon learn that he was not tired in the least, and that his slowness was entirely deliberate.

The next morning she fell into step beside Samir, fidgeting like a horse that has been tied to a post. He asked her in a mild voice where she was going, and when she answered, a little crossly, that she was going nowhere in particular, he nodded and asked why she was hurrying. Hana opened her mouth to reply and found, to her considerable surprise, that she had no answer at all.

Samir explained that most of us treat walking as a bridge between two places, something to be finished as quickly as possible so that real life can begin. He suggested, in his unhurried way, that every step is already a place, and that a person could arrive again and again with each foot that touches the ground. Hana thought it sounded rather like a riddle from a fairy tale, but she found that she did not dislike it.

Before they took a single step, Samir asked Hana to stand still, close her eyes and feel the soles of her feet against the earth. She was astonished by how much there was to notice, from the pressure under her heels and the stretch in her toes to the faint, constant movement of her weight as she swayed. It was the first time in forty years that she had stood and not been about to go somewhere.

Samir showed her a rhythm so simple that she was embarrassed to have missed it: one slow step as the air came in, and another as it went out, with no forcing of the breath at all. They moved along the riverbank like two people keeping time with a very gentle clock, and after a few minutes Hana found that her shoulders had dropped. She was walking slowly and, to her great surprise, she was actually enjoying it, which she would never have believed a week before.

Almost as soon as she began to walk slowly, Hana's head filled with lists, the shopping, the bills, the gutters, the call she still had to make to the dentist. Each time she noticed that she was miles away in her head, she brought her attention back to her feet and her breath, as one might bring a kite down to earth. It was less like a battle and more like a very patient game, with no winner and no final score.

At the bench beside the willow, Samir told her that a healthy adult at rest breathes in and out about twelve to twenty times in every minute, which comes to many thousands of breaths each day. We take almost all of them without noticing, he said, and yet they are among the few things that we always carry with us. Hana did the sum in her head, as a postwoman will, and was genuinely startled by the size of the answer.

Breathing, Samir pointed out, is an unusual kind of activity, for it goes on by itself while we sleep and yet it can be taken in hand whenever we wish. Few other things in the body work like this, and that may be why attention to the breath has been used as a doorway into stillness for so many centuries. It stands between the automatic and the chosen, like a gate that opens both ways.

Under the lungs, Samir explained, lies a broad, dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm, and it is the main engine of every calm breath. When it tightens and moves downward, the lungs are able to fill, and the belly swells outward a little as the organs below make room for it. Many people breathe only in the top of their chests, but with attention the whole body can join in.

Hana sat on the bench with one palm resting on her stomach and the other on her chest, and breathed in as slowly as she could without strain. She felt the lower hand lift gently like a boat on a swell, while the upper hand barely moved at all, and she let a long sigh out through her lips. It was not a trick or a technique, only a different way of attending to something she had done all her life.

Samir taught her that making the out-breath a little longer than the in-breath helps many people to feel calmer and less tense, and he said that this is why we sigh with relief. Research suggests that slow breathing can settle the body, although the studies are not all the same and it is certainly not a treatment for any illness. He liked it, he said, because it costs nothing, needs no equipment and does no harm when it is done gently.

On their walks, Samir gently encouraged her to breathe through her nose when it felt comfortable, since the nose warms the incoming air, makes it moist and catches some of the dust and tiny particles that float in it. The mouth has its uses as well, he said, especially in hard exercise or when the nose is blocked, so he was not making a rule of it. Hana felt that his habit of explaining without insisting was part of his charm.

One morning Samir suggested a simple count for the slow walk: breathe in over four steps and out over six, and let the numbers fall away whenever they start to feel like a chore. If she felt dizzy or breathless, he added, she should stop at once, rest and breathe normally. It was meant to be easy, he said, and anything that felt like straining was a signal to ease off.

Samir had only one rule, and he repeated it often, in the same quiet tone: never force the breath. If a pattern ever made her feel uneasy or lightheaded, she was free to drop it at once and simply breathe in whatever way felt natural. Comfort, he said, is not an obstacle to the practice but the foundation on which it stands.

Moving at Samir's pace, Hana became aware of the small journey that each foot made, from the heel touching down to the long roll along the arch and the final push from the toes. In forty years of walking, she had never once paid attention to this movement, and she marvelled at the quiet cleverness of her own body. A step that had once been a means to an end now seemed a small piece of choreography.

At the bend in the path they stopped, closed their eyes and listened, and Hana gradually became aware of how many different sounds were in the air around her. There was the chuckle of water running over stones, the liquid song of a blackbird high in the willow and the long, dry whisper of the wind moving through the reeds. They had been there all the time, she thought, and she had been walking past them.

Samir asked her to choose any leaf and to look at it as though she were an artist who had been paid to paint it, and Hana picked a broad one from the hazel at the water's edge. She saw the branching pattern of its veins, the tiny holes where an insect had been eating and the green light that glowed through it when she held it up to the sun. She had delivered post past this tree for decades and had never truly looked at it.

After a sudden spring shower, the whole river bank smelled of wet earth and wild garlic and the sharp, clean scent of new leaves. Hana stopped in the middle of the path, breathed in as deeply as she could and was overtaken by a flood of memories of her grandmother's garden. Smell, she reflected, goes straight to places that thought can never reach, and it opens doors that we had quite forgotten.

On the open stretch beyond the bridge, Hana held out both hands and let the morning sun settle on them like a gentle weight, while a cool wind moved over her cheeks and through her hair. It was strange to feel warmth and coolness together, and stranger still to realise how seldom she had taken the time to notice either. The weather had always been something that happened to her post round, she thought, and never something to be enjoyed.

Samir proposed a little game for the following week, in which Hana would choose one sense each day and walk with that sense awake and eager, leaving the others to take care of themselves. Monday would be hearing, Tuesday seeing and Wednesday touch, and on Thursday she might taste a cup of tea on the bench by the bridge. By Friday the whole world had begun to feel richer, as though somebody had turned up the colours.

Time after time, Hana found that she had drifted away from the path into thoughts about the past, her pension, the neighbours or the price of eggs. At first she scolded herself, but then she began to smile, say hello to the thought and return to her feet and her breath without any blame. It occurred to her that this gentleness was something she had never been taught to give herself.

One grey morning it rained steadily, and Hana's first instinct was to turn back to the warmth of her kitchen. Samir only smiled and put up his umbrella, and as they walked she noticed the cold touch of each drop, the soft drumming on the cloth and the way her irritation faded as she stopped arguing with the weather. The rain was not unpleasant, she discovered, once she stopped insisting that it should not be raining.

One morning Hana left her old postal watch on the kitchen table, half expecting to feel anxious without it, and instead she felt a faint, unfamiliar lightness. By the end of that week she had hardly missed it, and her days seemed somehow longer and more spacious than when she had measured every minute. It was a small thing, but it changed the way that she thought about time.

Hana confessed to Samir that she sometimes felt guilty, as though slow walking were a polite word for laziness, and he laughed out loud. The practice, he said, is not about speed at all but about being present, so there are times to hurry, such as when a bus is leaving, and there are times to slow down. What mattered was that she should choose her pace with open eyes, and not simply be swept along by habit.

In many Buddhist monasteries, Samir told her, monks alternate periods of sitting in silence with periods of very slow walking, in which they pace up and down a short path and give their whole attention to each footstep. The practice has different names and forms in different traditions, such as kinhin in Zen, and it is both a rest from sitting and a form of meditation in its own right. Hana was delighted to find that her slow river walk had such an ancient ancestry.

Walking has long been bound up with spiritual life, Samir said, and he told her about pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago in Spain, a route of about eight hundred kilometres on its French Way. Muslims on pilgrimage to Mecca walk seven times around the Kaaba, and many other traditions have their own sacred roads. Hana thought of her old postal round and wondered, with a smile, whether it had been her own small pilgrimage.

Samir described the great stone labyrinth in the floor of Chartres Cathedral in France, which dates from about the year 1200, and which visitors still walk slowly along its single winding path to the centre. Unlike a maze, he explained, it has no dead ends and no tricks, so the walker does not have to decide anything and can use the time to think, pray or simply be quiet. The point of such a walk, Samir said, is not to arrive anywhere but to let the walking itself become a kind of prayer.

Samir told her something that she found curious, which is that in several ancient languages the word for spirit is also the word for breath or wind, as in the Latin spiritus, the Hebrew ruach and the Greek pneuma. In Sanskrit the word prana is linked to breath and life energy, and traditions that were far apart in place and time seem to have noticed the same closeness. Hana wondered whether people have always felt, as she now did, that breath is something more than air.

When Hana's granddaughter Mei came to stay, she took one look at the slow walk and turned it into a game in which the winner was whoever could move most slowly without ever stopping. They crept along the bank like two enormous snails, giggling at every wobble and pausing now and then to inspect a beetle or a stone, and Hana realised that children are often better at this than grown-ups. Mei never once asked what time it was, and for that whole morning Hana did not think about it either.

At home that evening, Hana climbed the stairs of her small house with the same attention she had given to the river path, feeling each foot meet the wood and each leg lift its share of her weight. By the top she was breathing more evenly than she did when she hurried, and she wondered how many daily moments like this she had been rushing through. Even an ordinary staircase in an ordinary house, she decided, can become a path if one walks it with attention.

Waiting for the bus had once been a small torment to Hana, who would sigh, glare down the road and check a watch that she no longer wore. Now she stood with her feet comfortably apart, took three slow, unforced breaths and looked at the clouds drifting over the rooftops, so that the minutes passed without her noticing them. The bus came when it came, exactly as it had always done, and Hana was quite surprised to find that she did not mind.

It was a year since Hana had spoken to her sister Edith, following a quarrel over their mother's house that neither of them could now fully remember. One quiet morning she sat down beside the telephone, set both feet on the floor and took several slow breaths, letting her out-breath grow long and loose. Her hands were still unsteady when she picked up the receiver, but her mind was a little clearer than before.

Edith answered on the third ring, and for a moment neither sister could find a single word, so Hana breathed and let the silence be. The conversation that followed was awkward and halting, yet it was also warm, and by the end of it they had agreed to meet at the weekend for a cup of tea. Breathing had not mended anything, but it had given her enough steadiness to try.

On the anniversary of her husband's death, Hana walked along the river with her sadness beside her like a companion, and she did not try to drive it away. Slow breathing did not take the grief from her heart, but it gave the feeling space in which to move, and she cried a little without feeling that she was falling. Samir had said that if grief grew too heavy to carry alone, she must tell someone, perhaps a friend or a doctor.

A cyclist swept round the corner so close to Hana that his handlebar brushed her sleeve, and a wave of hot anger surged up in her. Instead of shouting after him, she stood still, took one long breath and allowed the out-breath to carry some of the heat away, and by the time she had finished, the cyclist was out of sight. She was still annoyed, as anyone would be, but she was no longer ruled by the annoyance, and that felt like a small victory.

At home, Hana took her time watering the pots on her balcony, noticing the weight of the can, the silver stream of the water and the darkening of the soil as it drank. The geraniums gave off a sharp green smell when she brushed them, and she smiled at the sparrow that came to watch from the railing. It was an ordinary chore that nobody would ever notice, but she did it as though it mattered, and in a way it did.

Some mornings Hana felt heavy and tired, and on one of them she apologised to Samir for dragging her feet. He told her cheerfully that rest was part of the practice, and that there was nothing to apologise for, because a body that needed a bench was entitled to use one. The whole point of attention, he said, is to listen to what the body is actually saying.

Mrs Okoro, who lived two doors away and had a lifelong problem with asthma, asked Samir whether slow breathing might replace her inhaler, and his answer was immediate and firm. Gentle breathing could be pleasant and calming, he said, but it was never a substitute for medicine, and anyone with difficulty breathing should see a doctor and follow their advice. Hana was glad to hear him say it so plainly, because she knew how easily gentle practices can be oversold.

On a clear morning in early summer, Hana and Samir climbed the green hill behind the town, taking each step in time with a slow, easy breath and stopping whenever the view invited them to. The slope that had looked so tiring from the bridge turned out to be perfectly manageable when it was taken one step at a time, and they reached the top without any struggle. Below them the river shone like a long thread of silver, winding between the fields and the first roofs of the town.

From the top of the hill, Hana could see the entire path of the river, the grey rooftops of the town and the bridge where she had first learned to stand still. She felt a deep, quiet satisfaction, and she thought that the view was somehow sweeter for having been reached slowly, one breath at a time. It struck her that she would have missed it all if she had still been running.

Sitting on a rock at the top of the hill, Samir told Hana that he had once been the most hurried carpenter in the county, always racing to finish one job so that he could begin the next. His grandfather, who walked as slowly as a river in summer, had taught him to take one step at a time and to notice what was in front of him. He had only really understood the lesson after he retired, when there was finally nobody left to hurry for.

Word of the slow walks spread along the street, and soon Mrs Okoro began to join them with her small, impatient dog, Biscuit, who was visibly puzzled by the pace. A teenage boy called Teo came as well, with his headphones round his neck, and he explained that he was only there because his mother had asked him to. By the end of the month he was, rather to his own amusement, the first one to arrive at the bridge.

On some mornings the little group did not say a single word, and Hana found, to her surprise, that the silence between them felt more like companionship than emptiness. They breathed and stepped together almost without meaning to, like a flock of birds turning in the same direction, and the river kept them company. She felt closer to these three people than to many she had talked to for years.

One warm summer evening the group walked beside the river after dark, past the lamps along the bank, whose lights lay in long yellow ribbons across the water. The streets were nearly empty, the air smelled of cut grass and woodsmoke, and one by one the stars came out above the hill as though somebody were slowly lighting them. They spoke in whispers, as one does in a church, and walked even more slowly than they usually did in the morning.

By December the river path was white with frost, and every breath that Hana and her friends exhaled rose before them as a small silver cloud that hung in the air for a moment before it faded. She found it wonderful to see, at last, the very thing that she had been paying attention to all year. They walked wrapped up in thick scarves and woollen hats, with cold noses and warm hearts, and nobody wished to be anywhere else.

In January Hana caught a heavy cold and stayed in bed for the better part of a week, unable to walk anywhere and slightly afraid that she would lose what she had learned. When she returned to the river, however, the path was exactly where she had left it, and Samir greeted her with a smile and a flask of tea. The practice, she saw, does not run away when we miss a few days.

By now the walk had spilled over into the rest of her day, and Hana had made three small rules: three slow breaths at the door, three before answering the phone and three at the table. They took no more than a minute altogether, yet they made her day feel as though it were punctuated by small, quiet pauses. She felt that she was living her own life instead of dashing through it.

When the blossom returned to the river path a year after her first slow walk, Samir told Hana that the path had never been intended to get her anywhere and that its only purpose was the walking. She laughed, because she finally understood him, and she took her granddaughter Mei by the hand and led her slowly on beside the water. A girl of seven and a woman of sixty-five walked on at the pace of snails, in no hurry at all.

That is all there is to it: walk slowly, breathe without force, notice the world around you and arrive again and again at each step, for as long as it feels good to do so. If you have trouble breathing, or if you feel very low or anxious for a long time, please speak to a doctor.
